questions.question: Two years after saphenous vein harvest, a patient presents with left leg swelling, erythema, and pain.
questions.question_raw: He presents with L leg swelling, erythema, pain 2 years later

parts.text: What is the most likely organism?
What are 3 interventions to decrease the risk of recurrence of this complication?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely organism?
What are 3 interventions to decrease the risk of recurrence of this complication.

questions.model_answer: a) Recurrent cellulitis of the ipsilateral leg due to impaired lymphatic/venous drainage from saphenous vein harvest (predisposing edema). b) β-hemolytic streptococci (group A or non-group A). c) (1) Treat and prevent interdigital tinea pedis with topical antifungals and maintain skin hygiene. (2) Reduce edema with support/compression stockings and elevation (pneumatic lymphatic compression if lymphedema). (3) Antibiotic prophylaxis for persistent recurrences — monthly benzathine penicillin or oral penicillin V (erythromycin if penicillin-allergic).

questions.question: A man with nodular lymphangitis who keeps an aquarium.
questions.question_raw: [image-based question: Picture of man with nodular lymphangitis. Has aquarium.]

parts.text: Give a differential of four possible causes of this clinical picture.
Given that he has an aquarium, which is most likely?

parts_raw.text: Give a differential of four possible causes of this clinical picture.
Given that he has an aquarium, which is most likely?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Mycobacterium marinum (2) Sporothrix schenckii (3) Nocardia brasiliensis (4) Leishmania braziliensis (also Francisella tularensis). b) Mycobacterium marinum (fish-tank/aquarium exposure). c) Skin biopsy of a lesion for histopathology plus mycobacterial culture at 30-32 C (with AFB stain); culture is the diagnostic standard.
questions.beyond_mandell: M. marinum and nodular-lymphangitis differential are outside this Sporothrix slice; based on standard mycobacterial/IDSA teaching.

cohort_answer.text: Differential: Mycobacterium marinum; Sporothrix schenckii; Nocardia brasiliensis; Leishmania braziliensis; Tularemia; Systemic mycoses. Most likely: Mycobacterium marinum. Diagnosis: Biopsy for AFB and culture + histopath. Treatment: surgical debridement/excision should suffice, if invasive, give rifampin + ethambutol +/- macrolide

questions.question: A child presents with enlargement of a single cervical lymph node.
questions.question_raw: Child with single cervical LN enlargement.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen (to species)?
How do you make the diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely pathogen (to species)?
How do you make the diagnosis?

questions.model_answer:
a) Nontuberculous mycobacteria, most commonly Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex (MAC) — now the principal cause of cervicofacial mycobacterial lymphadenitis in otherwise healthy young children, typically a unilateral submandibular/anterior cervical node with indolent progression over 1-3 months.
b) Excisional (complete) node biopsy for histopathology plus acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture, and species identification (gene sequencing for uncommon species). Excisional biopsy gives the highest microbiologic yield (up to ~90%), and identifying the species is critical because management differs for M. tuberculosis versus NTM.
c) Surgical excision of the involved fluctuant node(s) is the treatment of choice — for both cure and recovery of the organism for susceptibility testing — since NTM are frequently resistant to conventional antituberculous drugs. Adjunctive rifampin plus clarithromycin is considered when complete excision is precluded (e.g., extensive deep involvement, or submandibular nodes abutting the facial nerve).

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Mycobacterium avium complex. Diagnosis: Biopsy for AFB culture/histopathology. Optimal management: Surgical resection; if abx needed: Clarithromycin, rifampin/ethambutol

questions.question: A 24-year-old man has a warm, erythematous, fluctuant left neck mass and is febrile. For each of the following variants, name the most likely pathogen and the MOST APPROPRIATE sample and method of diagnosis.
questions.question_raw: 24-year old with left neck fluctuant mass. It is warm, and erythematous and the patient is febrile. Name the pathogen and the MOST APPROPRIATE sample and method of diagnosis.

parts.text: Variant: he was bitten in the neck by a rabbit.
Variant: he has just immigrated from the Philippines and also describes weight loss.
Variant: he ate steak tartare 1 week prior.
Variant: he has a sore throat with exudate.

parts_raw.text: Variant: He was bit in the neck by a rabbit
Variant: He just immigrated from the Phillipines and also describes weight loss.
Variant: He ate steak tartare 1 week prior
Variant: He has a sore throat with exudate

questions.model_answer:
a) Francisella tularensis (tularemia; rabbit exposure, glandular/ulceroglandular). Diagnosis: serology (paired acute/convalescent agglutinating antibody titers) is the mainstay; if culture of a node aspirate is attempted, alert the laboratory, as F. tularensis is highly hazardous and needs special handling.
b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (scrofula; recent immigrant from an endemic region with weight loss). Sample/method: fine-needle aspiration of the node for acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture, and NAAT — FNA recovers M. tuberculosis in >60% of cases in high-endemic settings and is less invasive; excisional biopsy (yield up to ~90%) if FNA is non-diagnostic.
c) Toxoplasma gondii (acute toxoplasmic lymphadenitis; raw-meat ingestion). Sample/method: serology, not biopsy — seroconversion or a fourfold rise in IgG, positive IgM ELISA, or a single Sabin-Feldman dye titer >=1:1024; a negative Toxoplasma IgG essentially excludes the diagnosis.
d) Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — suppurative cervical lymphadenitis following exudative pharyngitis/tonsillitis. Sample/method: throat swab for culture/rapid antigen plus Gram stain and culture of aspirated/drained node material; anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers support the diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Tularemia diagnostic approach (serology as mainstay, laboratory biosafety alert for culture) rests on CDC/standard ID guidance; the chapter names the rabbit/tularemia association but not its specific diagnostic test.

questions.question: A child from Ottawa with a swollen cervical lymph node whose biopsy shows caseating granuloma and is not improving on antibiotics.
questions.question_raw: Kid from Ottawa with swollen cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows caseating granuloma. Not improving on antibiotics.

parts.text: What is the treatment of choice?

parts_raw.text: What is the treatment of choice?

questions.model_answer: a) Nontuberculous mycobacteria - most commonly Mycobacterium avium complex (also Mycobacterium scrofulaceum) - the typical cause of chronic granulomatous cervical lymphadenitis in an otherwise healthy young Canadian child (Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains on the differential). b) Complete surgical excision of the involved node(s) is the treatment of choice; antimycobacterial drugs are adjunctive/reserved for incomplete resection or extensive disease.
questions.beyond_mandell: NTM lymphadenitis and its surgical management are not covered in this M. tuberculosis chapter (established pediatric ID knowledge).

cohort_answer.text: NTM (MAC, M. scrofulaceum) or TB (non-caseating granuloma ddx includes Bartonella, Toxoplasma, Syphilis, EBV, Tularemia, dimorphic fungi, Cryptococcus). Treatment of choice: Surgical resection

questions.question: A previously well 6-year-old presents with unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy and a history of trauma to her thigh. The lymph node is sampled and grows a beaded, branching gram-positive bacillus.
questions.question_raw: There is a previously well 6-year-old who presents with unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, with a history of trauma to her thigh. The LN is sampled and grows a beading branching GPB.

parts.text: What is the most likely cause (genus only)?
Name three antibiotics that will cover it.

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely cause (Genus only)
Three antibiotics that will cover it.

questions.model_answer: a) Actinomyces (e.g., Actinomyces israelii) - a beaded, branching, filamentous gram-positive bacillus. b) (1) Penicillin G; (2) Amoxicillin/ampicillin; (3) Ceftriaxone. (Non-beta-lactam alternatives include doxycycline or clindamycin.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Actinomyces identification and treatment are from established microbiology/Mandell Actinomycosis chapter; this Bartonella text slice contains no source for this question.

cohort_answer.text: Cause: Actinomyces (israelii). Antibiotics: Penicillin G; Amoxicillin; Ceftriaxone (if non-beta lactam: doxy, clinda)
